title: Iunonis ira. Aeolus
titleEn: Juno's Anger and the Storm — Aeneid I.1–101
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The opening of the Aeneid. Virgil names his subject — war, and a man driven by fate from Troy to Italy to found the line that leads to Rome — and asks the Muse why the queen of the gods hated so good a man. Then the story begins, in the middle: the Trojans are leaving Sicily, seven years after Troy fell, when Juno, nursing her grievances, goes to Aeolus, keeper of the winds, and bribes him with a nymph to wreck their fleet. The storm breaks, and Aeneas, named for the first time ninety-two lines in, wishes he had died fighting at Troy. Virgil writes in dactylic hexameter, the metre of Homer, and he writes against Homer throughout: the storm, the hero's despair and the keeper of the winds all come from the Odyssey, retold for Rome.

sentences.t:
Arma virumque cano, Troiae qui primus ab oris
Italiam, fato profugus, Laviniaque venit
litora, multum ille et terris iactatus et alto
vi superum saevae memorem Iunonis ob iram;
sentences.l:
Arms and a man I sing, who first from the shores of Troy
to Italy, by fate a fugitive, and to the Lavinian came
shores — much tossed was he, both on lands and on the deep,
by the force of those above, for savage Juno's mindful anger;
sentences.i: War is my song, and a man — the one who first came from the coasts of Troy, an exile by fate's decree, to Italy and the shores of Lavinium, much buffeted on land and sea by the power of the gods because of savage Juno's anger, which would not forget;
sentences.n: The poem's first words name its two halves: 'arma', war (the fighting in Italy, Books 7–12), and 'virum', the man (his wanderings, Books 1–6) — Homer's two poems in reverse order, the Iliad of war and the Odyssey, whose first word is 'man'. 'cano' (I sing) is the poet speaking in his own voice; Homer asked the Muse to sing. Aeneas is not named until line 92: until then he is 'the man', 'ille'. 'Italiam' and 'litora' are accusatives of goal without a preposition, ordinary in verse. 'superum' = 'superorum', the old short genitive plural (you'll see this constantly: 'divom', 'virum', 'Danaum'). 'memorem' grammatically belongs to 'iram': the anger itself remembers, a transferred epithet. 'Laviniaque' is read with the second i as a consonant, La-vin-ja-que.

sentences.t:
multa quoque et bello passus, dum conderet urbem,
inferretque deos Latio, genus unde Latinum,
Albanique patres, atque altae moenia Romae.
sentences.l:
many things also in war having suffered, until he should found a city
and bring his gods into Latium — whence the Latin race,
and the Alban fathers, and the walls of lofty Rome.
sentences.i: and much he suffered in war as well, until he could found a city and bring his gods to Latium — the beginning of the Latin race, the fathers of Alba, and the walls of towering Rome.
sentences.n: 'dum conderet' — 'dum' with the subjunctive means 'until', looking ahead to a goal not yet reached: when the poem begins, the city is still to come. 'deos' are the Penates, Troy's household gods, which Aeneas carries out of the burning city; bringing them to Latium is the religious heart of his mission. 'genus unde Latinum' — 'from where (comes) the Latin race'; the verb is left out. The sentence runs in three stages from Aeneas to the city of Virgil's own day: Lavinium, then Alba Longa (founded by his son), then Rome.

sentences.t:
Musa, mihi causas memora, quo numine laeso,
quidve dolens, regina deum tot volvere casus
insignem pietate virum, tot adire labores
impulerit.
sentences.l:
Muse, to me recount the causes: by what divine will offended,
or grieving at what, the queen of the gods to roll through so many misfortunes
a man famed for devotion, to face so many toils,
compelled.
sentences.i: Muse, tell me the causes: what offence to her divinity, what grievance drove the queen of the gods to send a man marked out by his sense of duty through so many turns of fortune, to face so many trials.
sentences.n: Virgil states his theme first and only then calls on the Muse; Homer opens with the Muse. 'memora' — 'remind me, recount': the Muse is the memory of the past. 'quo numine laeso' is an ablative absolute, 'what divine will (of hers) having been injured'; 'numen' is a god's power and will. 'deum' = 'deorum'. 'volvere casus' — 'to roll through misfortunes', the picture of a cycle of events turning. 'pietate' names Aeneas's defining quality: 'pietas' is duty to gods, family and country, much wider than English 'piety'. 'impulerit' (perfect subjunctive in an indirect question) is held to the start of line 11, so the whole question hangs until its verb arrives.

sentences.t: Tantaene animis caelestibus irae?
sentences.l: Are there such great angers to heavenly spirits?
sentences.i: Can the spirits of heaven harbour such anger?
sentences.n: One of the poem's most quoted lines. 'animis caelestibus' is a dative of possession — 'are there to heavenly minds such angers?' — with 'sunt' understood. The plural 'irae' is idiomatic: fits of anger, resentments. The question is a real one, and the poem never answers it comfortably.

sentences.i: An old city once stood, Carthage, where settlers from Tyre made their home, facing Italy and the mouth of the Tiber far away, rich in wealth and fierce beyond all others in the arts of war.
sentences.n: 'antiqua' is ancient from Virgil's point of view; in Aeneas's day Carthage is still being built. 'tenuere' = 'tenuerunt', the poetic 3rd-plural perfect (you'll see this constantly). 'Karthago' with K is Greenough's spelling. 'contra' follows its noun ('Italiam contra'), and 'longe' covers both: Carthage faces Italy across a wide sea. 'opum' is genitive with 'dives' (rich in), 'studiis belli' ablative of respect with 'asperrima'. Virgil's readers knew how this ended: three wars with Rome, and Carthage razed in 146 BCE.

sentences.t:
quam Iuno fertur terris magis omnibus unam
posthabita coluisse Samo;
sentences.l:
which Juno is said, more than all lands, alone
to have cherished, with Samos placed second;
sentences.i: Juno, it is said, loved this one city more than any land on earth, ranking even Samos below it.
sentences.n: 'fertur' — 'she is said' — the poet hands the story on as received tradition. 'quam… unam' — 'which one city' — frames the clause. 'posthabita Samo' is an ablative absolute, 'with Samos held second'; Samos, an island off Asia Minor, had the great temple of Juno (Hera to the Greeks). Carthage's own chief goddess was identified with Juno, which is why a Roman poet makes Carthage Juno's city.

sentences.t:
hic illius arma,
hic currus fuit; hoc regnum dea gentibus esse,
si qua fata sinant, iam tum tenditque fovetque.
sentences.l:
here her arms,
here her chariot was; that this be the ruling power over the nations, the goddess,
if in any way the fates allow, already then both strives and fosters.
sentences.i: Here were her arms, here her chariot; even then, if the fates would somehow permit it, the goddess was set on making this city sovereign over the nations, and nursed the hope.
sentences.n: 'hic… hic' — the repeated adverb marks her attachment. 'fuit' is singular with two subjects, agreeing with the nearer. 'hoc' takes the gender of 'regnum' ('that this should be the kingdom'). 'si qua' — 'if in any way'; 'qua' is the adverb here, not the pronoun. 'tendit' (strains, aims) and 'fovet' (warms, cherishes) are vivid presents: 'even then she is striving and nursing it'. The double '-que… -que' ('both… and') is an epic mannerism you will meet again and again.

sentences.t:
Progeniem sed enim Troiano a sanguine duci
audierat, Tyrias olim quae verteret arces;
hinc populum late regem belloque superbum
venturum excidio Libyae: sic volvere Parcas.
sentences.i: But she had heard that a race was springing from Trojan blood that would one day overthrow the towers of Tyre; from it would come a people ruling far and wide and proud in war, to be the ruin of Libya. So the Fates were spinning it.
sentences.n: 'sed enim' — 'but in truth', an archaic pair; note it stands second in its clause. 'duci' is present passive infinitive, 'was being drawn (descended)', depending on 'audierat'. 'quae verteret' is a relative clause of purpose, 'such as to overturn'. 'late regem' — 'regem' used like an adjective, 'king far and wide'. 'excidio Libyae' — a double dative, 'for a destruction to Libya'. 'volvere Parcas' is still reported speech, accusative and infinitive; the Parcae are the Fates, who turn the thread of destiny on the spindle. 'Libya' stands for Africa, as in Latin poetry generally.

sentences.t:
Id metuens, veterisque memor Saturnia belli,
prima quod ad Troiam pro caris gesserat Argis—
sentences.l:
This fearing, and mindful of the old war, the daughter of Saturn,
which foremost at Troy for dear Argos she had waged —
sentences.i: Fearing this, and remembering the old war she had fought at Troy as champion of her beloved Argives, Saturn's daughter —
sentences.n: 'Saturnia' — Juno as daughter of Saturn, a title that recalls an older, harsher order of gods. 'prima' most likely means she was foremost in that war. 'Argis' ('Argos', plural in form) stands for the Greeks generally. The sentence breaks off at the dash: Virgil stops to list her grievances, and the main verb of 'Saturnia' does not arrive until 'arcebat' in line 31.

sentences.t:
necdum etiam causae irarum saevique dolores
exciderant animo:
sentences.l:
nor yet even had the causes of her angers and her savage griefs
fallen from her mind:
sentences.i: nor had the causes of her anger and her bitter grief yet faded from her mind;
sentences.n: 'exciderant' is from 'excido' (ex + cado), 'to fall out (of)'; the pluperfect looks back from the moment of the story. 'animo' is ablative of separation: 'fallen from her mind'. 'causae irarum' is read run together, 'caus' irarum': a final vowel before a word beginning with a vowel is slurred into it (elision — you'll see this constantly in Latin verse).

sentences.t:
manet alta mente repostum
iudicium Paridis spretaeque iniuria formae,
et genus invisum, et rapti Ganymedis honores.
sentences.l:
there remains, laid up deep in her mind,
the judgement of Paris and the wrong to her spurned beauty,
and the hated race, and the honours of snatched-away Ganymede.
sentences.i: deep in her heart lay stored the judgement of Paris and the insult to her slighted beauty, the race she hated, and the honours paid to Ganymede, carried off to heaven.
sentences.n: 'repostum' = 'repositum', shortened for the metre: 'stored away'. Three grievances. Paris judged Venus fairer than Juno ('spretae formae', her beauty scorned). The Trojans descend from Dardanus, Jupiter's son by another woman ('genus invisum'). And Jupiter carried off the Trojan boy Ganymede — in the usual telling, as his beloved — and made him cupbearer of the gods in heaven. 'iniuria formae' is an objective genitive: the wrong done to her beauty. 'manet' is singular with a list of subjects, agreeing with the first.

sentences.t:
His accensa super, iactatos aequore toto
Troas, reliquias Danaum atque immitis Achilli,
arcebat longe Latio, multosque per annos
errabant, acti fatis, maria omnia circum.
sentences.l:
By these inflamed besides, the tossed-about-on-the-whole-sea
Trojans, the leavings of the Danaans and of pitiless Achilles,
she kept far from Latium, and through many years
they wandered, driven by the fates, around all the seas.
sentences.i: Inflamed by all this as well, she kept the Trojans far from Latium, tossed over the whole expanse of the sea — all that the Greeks and pitiless Achilles had left of them — and for many years they wandered, driven by the fates, across every sea.
sentences.n: 'super' is an adverb, 'in addition': these grievances were added to her fear for Carthage. 'Troas' is a Greek accusative plural, 'the Trojans'. 'reliquias Danaum' — 'the leftovers of the Greeks', those the Greeks had not killed. 'Achilli' is an old genitive of 'Achilles'. 'circum' follows its noun: 'maria omnia circum', 'around all the seas'. The imperfects 'arcebat… errabant' describe a long, continuing state, and 'acti fatis' sits beside them: Juno obstructs, but the fates drive.

sentences.t: Tantae molis erat Romanam condere gentem!
sentences.l: Of so great a mass it was to found the Roman nation!
sentences.i: Such a weight of toil it took to found the Roman nation!
sentences.n: The proem closes on a single line. 'tantae molis' is a genitive of description, 'a thing of such weight': 'moles' is a massive bulk, the word for a huge structure or a vast effort. The infinitive phrase 'Romanam condere gentem' is the subject of 'erat'. The line steps out of the myth into Virgil's own Rome.

sentences.t:
Vix e conspectu Siculae telluris in altum
vela dabant laeti, et spumas salis aere ruebant,
cum Iuno, aeternum servans sub pectore volnus,
haec secum:
sentences.l:
Hardly out of sight of the Sicilian land, into the deep
they were giving their sails, glad, and the foam of the salt with bronze were churning,
when Juno, an eternal wound keeping under her breast,
these words with herself:
sentences.i: They were barely out of sight of Sicily, joyfully spreading sail for the open sea and churning the salt foam with their bronze prows, when Juno, nursing the everlasting wound in her heart, said to herself:
sentences.n: The story starts in the middle, Homer's way: the Trojans are leaving Sicily in the seventh year of their wanderings; how they got there Aeneas tells in Books 2–3. 'vela dabant' — 'they were giving their sails (to the winds)'. 'aere' is ablative of 'aes', bronze: the bronze-sheathed prows. 'vix… cum' — 'hardly… when': the main event comes in the 'when' clause. 'volnus' is Greenough's older spelling of 'vulnus'. 'haec secum' — the verb of speaking is left out: '(she said) these things to herself'.

sentences.t:
“Mene incepto desistere victam,
nec posse Italia Teucrorum avertere regem?
sentences.l:
“That I, from what I began, should desist, defeated,
and not be able from Italy the king of the Teucrians to turn away?
sentences.i: “Am I to give up what I have begun, beaten, unable to keep the Trojan king away from Italy?
sentences.n: An exclamatory question in the accusative and infinitive: 'me… desistere' — '(am) I to give up?' — the infinitive of indignation, with '-ne' attached to 'me'. 'incepto' is ablative of separation with 'desistere'. 'Teucri' (from Teucer, an early king of Troy) is another name for the Trojans. Juno's first word is 'me'.

sentences.t: Quippe vetor fatis.
sentences.l: Of course — I am forbidden by the fates.
sentences.i: Naturally: the fates forbid me.
sentences.n: 'quippe' is bitterly sarcastic here, 'of course!' Juno quotes the excuse she knows will be thrown at her, and dismisses it in three words.

sentences.t:
Pallasne exurere classem
Argivum atque ipsos potuit submergere ponto,
unius ob noxam et furias Aiacis Oilei?
sentences.l:
Was Pallas able to burn up the fleet
of the Argives and the men themselves to sink in the sea,
because of the offence and the frenzy of one man, Ajax son of Oileus?
sentences.i: Could Pallas burn the Argive fleet and drown the men themselves in the sea for the crime and madness of one man, Ajax son of Oileus?
sentences.n: Pallas Athena wrecked the returning Greek fleet because the lesser Ajax (son of Oileus, not the great Ajax) dragged Cassandra from Athena's altar at the sack of Troy. Juno's point: a lesser goddess was allowed that much. 'Pallasne' — the question particle '-ne' on the first word. 'Argivum' = 'Argivorum'. 'Oilei' is a Greek genitive, read O-i-lei.

sentences.t:
Ipsa, Iovis rapidum iaculata e nubibus ignem,
disiecitque rates evertitque aequora ventis,
illum expirantem transfixo pectore flammas
turbine corripuit scopuloque infixit acuto.
sentences.l:
She herself, Jupiter's devouring fire having hurled from the clouds,
both scattered the ships and overturned the waters with winds;
him, breathing out from his pierced breast flames,
with a whirlwind she seized and on a sharp crag impaled.
sentences.i: She herself hurled Jupiter's devouring fire from the clouds, scattered their ships and churned up the sea with winds; and him, gasping out flames from his pierced chest, she caught up in a whirlwind and impaled on a jagged rock.
sentences.n: 'Ipsa' — she herself, with her own hands — is the sting. 'Iovis ignem' is the thunderbolt, normally Jupiter's alone. 'rapidum' is 'snatching, consuming' (from 'rapio') as much as 'swift'. 'iaculata' is a deponent participle with active meaning, 'having hurled'. 'illum' is Ajax: the lightning has gone through his chest, and he breathes out its fire. 'disiecitque… evertitque' — the double '-que' again.

sentences.t:
Ast ego, quae divom incedo regina, Iovisque
et soror et coniunx, una cum gente tot annos
bella gero!
sentences.l:
But I, who as queen of the gods stride, of Jupiter
both sister and wife, with one nation for so many years
wars I wage!
sentences.i: Yet I, who walk in majesty as queen of the gods, Jupiter's sister and his wife, have been waging war on a single people for all these years!
sentences.n: 'ast' is the archaic, solemn form of 'at' (but). 'incedo' is the stately walk of a deity or a queen. 'divom' = 'divorum'. 'et soror et coniunx' — Juno and Jupiter are both children of Saturn. 'una cum gente' — 'with one people'; the emphasis is on 'una', a single nation. 'gero' is present with 'tot annos': Latin uses the present for an action that began in the past and is still going on, where English says 'have been waging'.

sentences.t:
Et quisquam numen Iunonis adoret
praeterea, aut supplex aris imponet honorem?”
sentences.l:
And will anyone the divinity of Juno worship
hereafter, or as a suppliant on her altars place an offering?”
sentences.i: Will anyone worship the godhead of Juno after this, or lay an offering on her altars as a suppliant?”
sentences.n: 'adoret' (present subjunctive, 'is anyone to worship?') and 'imponet' (future indicative, 'will anyone lay?') stand side by side; the shift sharpens the question. 'honorem' is concrete here: an offering, a sacrifice. Juno names herself in the third person — her standing as a goddess is what is at stake.

sentences.t:
Talia flammato secum dea corde volutans
nimborum in patriam, loca feta furentibus austris,
Aeoliam venit.
sentences.l:
Such things in her inflamed heart with herself the goddess turning over,
into the fatherland of storm-clouds, places teeming with raging south winds,
Aeolia she came.
sentences.i: Turning such thoughts over in her burning heart, the goddess came to Aeolia, homeland of the storm-clouds, a place teeming with raging winds.
sentences.n: 'flammato corde' — 'in her inflamed heart', ablative. 'volutans' — 'rolling over and over', the frequentative of 'volvo'. 'feta' means pregnant, teeming: the winds are bred there. 'austris' — properly the south winds, here winds in general. Aeolia is the island of Aeolus, keeper of the winds, a figure borrowed from the Odyssey, where Aeolus gives Odysseus the winds tied in a bag.

sentences.t:
Hic vasto rex Aeolus antro
luctantes ventos tempestatesque sonoras
imperio premit ac vinclis et carcere frenat.
sentences.l:
Here in a vast cave King Aeolus
the struggling winds and the sounding storms
with command presses and with chains and prison bridles.
sentences.i: Here in a vast cavern King Aeolus holds down the wrestling winds and the roaring gales by his authority, and curbs them with chains and a prison.
sentences.n: 'vasto antro' is ablative of place without a preposition, normal in verse. The line 'luctantes ventos tempestatesque sonoras' is heavy with long syllables, as if under strain. 'vinclis' = 'vinculis', shortened. 'frenat' — 'bridles' — pictures the winds as wild horses, a picture that returns in line 63. 'imperio' is a ruler's authority to command.

sentences.t:
Illi indignantes magno cum murmure montis
circum claustra fremunt;
sentences.l:
They, resenting it, with a great rumbling of the mountain
around the barriers roar;
sentences.i: They chafe and roar around the barriers, and the whole mountain rumbles with them;
sentences.n: 'indignantes' — resenting their confinement, as if the winds had pride. 'magno cum murmure montis' — listen to the run of m's, the sound of the rumble. 'circum claustra' — around the bars, the bolted doors of the cave-prison. 'Illi indignantes' is read run together, 'Ill' indignantes' (elision).

sentences.t:
celsa sedet Aeolus arce
sceptra tenens, mollitque animos et temperat iras.
sentences.l:
on a high citadel sits Aeolus
holding his sceptre, and softens their spirits and tempers their angers.
sentences.i: Aeolus sits in his high citadel, sceptre in hand, soothing their tempers and calming their rage.
sentences.n: 'celsa arce' — ablative of place again. 'sceptra' is plural for singular, common in verse. 'animos' — the winds have 'spirits', fittingly, since 'animus' and 'anima' meant breath and wind before they meant mind and soul. 'temperat iras' answers the question of line 11 about anger: Aeolus restrains here what Juno is about to set loose.

sentences.t:
Ni faciat, maria ac terras caelumque profundum
quippe ferant rapidi secum verrantque per auras.
sentences.l:
If he did not do it, the seas and lands and the deep sky
surely they would carry, rushing, with them and sweep through the air.
sentences.i: If he did not, they would surely carry off sea and land and the depths of the sky in their rush, and sweep them away through the air.
sentences.n: A condition contrary to fact with the present subjunctive ('ni faciat… ferant'), an older usage where classical prose would have the imperfect. 'ni' = 'nisi'. 'quippe' here is 'for of course, surely', with none of the sarcasm of line 39. 'caelum profundum' — the sky is 'deep', as the sea is. 'rapidi' — 'snatching, sweeping', the winds' own nature.

sentences.t:
Sed pater omnipotens speluncis abdidit atris,
hoc metuens, molemque et montis insuper altos
imposuit, regemque dedit, qui foedere certo
et premere et laxas sciret dare iussus habenas.
sentences.l:
But the father almighty in dark caves hid them away,
this fearing, and a mass and high mountains on top
set, and gave a king, who by a fixed compact
both to press and, when ordered, to give loose reins would know.
sentences.i: But the almighty father, fearing this, hid them away in dark caves, piled a mass of towering mountains over them, and gave them a king who would know, under fixed terms, when to rein them in and when, on command, to give them their head.
sentences.n: 'pater omnipotens' is Jupiter. 'molemque et montis altos' — 'a mass and high mountains', two nouns for one thing: 'a mass of high mountains'. 'montis' is accusative plural (= 'montes'), Greenough's -is spelling, which he uses often. 'foedere certo' — by a fixed compact: even Aeolus rules by agreement with Jupiter. 'laxas dare habenas' — 'to give loose reins', the horse image of line 54 again. 'iussus' — 'when ordered' — prepares what follows: Juno is about to give an order that is not hers to give.

sentences.t: Ad quem tum Iuno supplex his vocibus usa est:
sentences.l: To whom then Juno as a suppliant used these words:
sentences.i: To him Juno now made her plea in these words:
sentences.n: 'Ad quem' is a connecting relative, 'and to him' (you'll see this constantly). 'utor' takes the ablative: 'his vocibus usa est', 'used these words'. The queen of the gods, who has just boasted of walking in majesty, comes as a suppliant to a minor power.

sentences.t:
“Aeole, namque tibi divom pater atque hominum rex
et mulcere dedit fluctus et tollere vento,
gens inimica mihi Tyrrhenum navigat aequor,
Ilium in Italiam portans victosque Penates:
sentences.l:
“Aeolus — for to you the father of gods and king of men
has given both to soothe the waves and to raise them with wind —
a race hostile to me is sailing the Tyrrhenian sea,
Ilium into Italy carrying, and its conquered Penates:
sentences.i: “Aeolus — since the father of gods and king of men has given you power to calm the waves and to raise them with the wind — a people I hate is sailing the Tyrrhenian sea, carrying Ilium and its defeated household gods to Italy.
sentences.n: 'namque' gives the reason for addressing him before the request itself: a formal prayer begins by naming the god's power. 'divom pater atque hominum rex' is an old formula for Jupiter, already in Ennius. 'vento' is ablative of means. The 'Tyrrhenum aequor' is the sea west of Italy, the water they must cross to reach Latium. 'Ilium portans' — they carry Troy itself: its people and its gods, the Penates, whom Juno sneers at as 'victos', beaten gods.

sentences.t:
incute vim ventis submersasque obrue puppes,
aut age diversos et disiice corpora ponto.
sentences.l:
strike force into the winds and overwhelm the sunk sterns,
or drive them apart and scatter their bodies on the sea.
sentences.i: Lash the winds into fury, swamp their ships and sink them, or drive them apart and strew their bodies over the sea.
sentences.n: 'submersas obrue puppes' — 'overwhelm the sunk ships': the participle anticipates the result of the verb, 'overwhelm them so that they sink'. 'puppes' (sterns) stands for whole ships, the part for the whole. 'diversos' — 'in different directions'. 'disiice' is Greenough's spelling of 'disice' (from 'dis' + 'iacio'). 'ponto' — 'on the sea', ablative of place.

sentences.t:
Sunt mihi bis septem praestanti corpore nymphae,
quarum quae forma pulcherrima Deiopea,
conubio iungam stabili propriamque dicabo,
omnis ut tecum meritis pro talibus annos
exigat, et pulchra faciat te prole parentem.”
sentences.l:
There are to me twice seven nymphs of outstanding body,
of whom the one who in beauty is loveliest, Deiopea,
in marriage I will join to you, lasting, and as your own I will dedicate,
so that all her years with you, for such services,
she may spend, and with lovely offspring make you a parent.”
sentences.i: I have fourteen nymphs of surpassing beauty; the loveliest of them, Deiopea, I will join to you in lasting marriage and make your own, so that for such a service she may spend all her years with you and make you the father of beautiful children.”
sentences.n: 'Sunt mihi' — dative of possession, 'I have'. 'bis septem' — 'twice seven', a poetic way of counting. 'quarum quae forma pulcherrima' — 'of whom (the one) who is loveliest in beauty'; the name Deiopea is drawn into the relative clause, where we expect it as the object of 'iungam'. 'omnis annos' = 'omnes annos'. Juno is the goddess of marriage, so her bribe is a wedding, and she promises it in the language of lawful Roman marriage: 'conubio stabili', 'propriam'.

sentences.t:
Aeolus haec contra: “Tuus, O regina, quid optes
explorare labor;
sentences.l:
Aeolus these words in reply: “Yours, O queen, what you may wish
to search out is the task;
sentences.i: Aeolus answered her: “Your task, my queen, is to weigh what you want;
sentences.n: 'haec contra' — again the verb of speaking is left out: '(said) these things in reply'. 'Tuus labor (est)' — 'yours is the work', with the infinitive 'explorare' as its content: 'to search out what you wish'. 'optes' is subjunctive in an indirect question. 'O regina' — Aeolus addresses her by her title at once.

sentences.t: mihi iussa capessere fas est.
sentences.l: for me, to take up commands is right.
sentences.i: mine is to carry out your commands.
sentences.n: 'fas est' — 'it is right by divine law', a religious word. Aeolus' instant obedience ignores the condition in line 63: he was to give the winds their head only 'when ordered', and the order was meant to be Jupiter's. 'capessere' — to take hold of, to undertake eagerly.

sentences.t:
Tu mihi, quodcumque hoc regni, tu sceptra Iovemque
concilias, tu das epulis accumbere divom,
nimborumque facis tempestatumque potentem.”
sentences.l:
You for me, whatever this is of kingdom, you the sceptre and Jupiter
win over, you grant me to recline at the feasts of the gods,
and of storm-clouds you make me and of storms master.”
sentences.i: It is you who won me this kingdom, such as it is — you who won me the sceptre and Jupiter's favour; you let me recline at the banquets of the gods and make me lord of storm-clouds and tempests.”
sentences.n: 'Tu… tu… tu' — the repeated pronoun piles up his debts to her. 'quodcumque hoc regni' — partitive genitive, 'whatever this (amount) of kingdom (is)': a modest, half-apologetic phrase. 'concilias' — 'you procure, you win for me'. 'epulis' is dative with 'accumbere', to recline at the banquet, as Romans dined. 'potentem' with the genitive: 'master of'. In the Odyssey Aeolus is a mortal king dear to the gods; here he owes his place to Juno.

sentences.t:
Haec ubi dicta, cavum conversa cuspide montem
impulit in latus: ac venti, velut agmine facto,
qua data porta, ruunt et terras turbine perflant.
sentences.l:
These things when said, the hollow, with turned spear-point, mountain
he struck in its side: and the winds, as if a column had been formed,
where a gate is given, rush and the lands with a whirlwind blow through.
sentences.i: With these words he turned his spear and struck the hollow mountain on its side; and the winds, as if drawn up in battle column, rush out where an outlet is given and blast across the lands in a whirlwind.
sentences.n: 'Haec ubi dicta' — '(were) said', with 'sunt' left out, as often. 'cavum… montem' frames the line, with 'conversa cuspide' inside it: an ablative absolute, 'his spear turned', as he swings it round to strike. 'agmine facto' — a military picture: the winds burst out like an army formed in column. 'qua data porta' — 'where a gate (has been) given', where an opening has been made. 'ruunt… perflant' — vivid presents.

sentences.t:
Incubuere mari, totumque a sedibus imis
una Eurusque Notusque ruunt creberque procellis
Africus, et vastos volvunt ad litora fluctus.
sentences.l:
They have fallen on the sea, and the whole of it from its lowest seats
together both Eurus and Notus upheave, and, thick with squalls,
Africus, and vast toward the shores they roll the waves.
sentences.i: They swoop down upon the sea, and East wind and South wind together, and the squall-laden wind from Africa, heave it up from its deepest beds and roll huge waves toward the shores.
sentences.n: 'Incubuere' = 'incubuerunt', a perfect of sudden action: 'they have fallen on' before we see it happen. 'totum' agrees with 'mare', understood from 'mari'. 'ruunt' is transitive here, 'they churn up', where in line 83 it meant 'they rush'. Three winds — Eurus (east), Notus (south) and Africus (south-west, off Africa) — blow at once, an impossibility that marks this as no natural storm. 'creber procellis' — 'thick with squalls'. The scene is modelled on the storm Poseidon raises against Odysseus in Odyssey 5.

sentences.t: Insequitur clamorque virum stridorque rudentum.
sentences.l: There follows both the shouting of men and the shrieking of the ropes.
sentences.i: Then come the shouts of men and the screech of the rigging.
sentences.n: 'virum' = 'virorum', the old genitive plural again. 'clamorque… stridorque' — 'both… and', the two sounds set side by side: the men below, the ropes above. 'rudentes' are a ship's ropes and rigging, which shriek in the wind. 'Insequitur' stands first, singular, with two subjects to follow.

sentences.t:
Eripiunt subito nubes caelumque diemque
Teucrorum ex oculis;
sentences.l:
The clouds snatch suddenly both sky and day
from the eyes of the Teucrians;
sentences.i: All at once the clouds snatch sky and daylight from the Trojans' eyes;
sentences.n: 'nubes' is nominative plural, the subject, placed after the verb. 'caelumque diemque' — the double '-que' again, 'both sky and day'. 'Eripiunt' stands first for force: the clouds tear the light away. 'Teucrorum ex oculis' is read run together, 'Teucror' ex oculis' (elision).

sentences.t: ponto nox incubat atra.
sentences.l: on the sea a black night lies.
sentences.i: black night broods over the sea.
sentences.n: 'incubat' — 'lies upon, broods over' — is from the same verb as 'incubuere' in line 84: the winds fall on the sea, and now night settles on it. 'ponto' is dative with the compound verb. 'atra' agrees with 'nox' and is held to the end of the line.

sentences.t:
Intonuere poli, et crebris micat ignibus aether,
praesentemque viris intentant omnia mortem.
sentences.l:
The poles have thundered, and with frequent fires flashes the upper air,
and present to the men everything holds out death.
sentences.i: The vault of heaven thunders, the sky flickers with fire upon fire, and everything the men see threatens them with death close at hand.
sentences.n: 'poli' — the poles, the two ends of the sky's axis — stand for the whole heaven. 'Intonuere' = 'intonuerunt'. 'aether' is the bright upper air. 'praesentem… mortem' — death that is present, immediate — frames the line. 'intentant' — 'hold out (as a threat)', with the dative 'viris'.

sentences.t: Extemplo Aeneae solvuntur frigore membra:
sentences.l: At once Aeneas's limbs are loosened with chill:
sentences.i: At once Aeneas's limbs go slack with a chill of fear;
sentences.n: The hero's name comes at last, ninety-two lines into the poem — and he is introduced in terror. 'solvuntur membra' — 'his limbs are loosened' — is a Homeric phrase, used of Odysseus in his storm in Odyssey 5. 'frigore' is the chill of fear, not of weather. 'Aeneae' is genitive, read in three syllables, Ae-ne-ae.

sentences.t:
ingemit, et duplicis tendens ad sidera palmas
talia voce refert:
sentences.l:
he groans, and stretching to the stars his double palms,
such things with his voice he utters:
sentences.i: he groans, and stretching both his hands up to the stars he cries out:
sentences.n: 'duplicis palmas' = 'duplices', 'both his palms': hands stretched out palms upward are the gesture of prayer. 'ad sidera' — to the stars, though the sky is black. 'talia voce refert' — 'brings out such things with his voice', a formula introducing speech.

sentences.t:
“O terque quaterque beati,
quis ante ora patrum Troiae sub moenibus altis
contigit oppetere!
sentences.l:
“O both three-times and four-times blessed,
to whom it befell before the faces of their fathers beneath the high walls of Troy
to meet death!
sentences.i: “How fortunate, three times and four times over, were those whose lot it was to die beneath the high walls of Troy, before their fathers' eyes!
sentences.n: 'terque… quaterque' — 'both three times and four times', the paired '-que' again. Aeneas's first words echo Odysseus in his storm in Odyssey 5 ('three times blessed the Greeks, and four times, who died at Troy'), and the reader is meant to hear it. 'quis' = 'quibus', dative with 'contigit', 'it fell to them'. 'ante ora patrum' — 'before their fathers' faces': to die in plain sight, with honour and burial, unlike drowning unseen. 'oppetere' — 'to meet (death)', with 'mortem' understood.

sentences.t:
O Danaum fortissime gentis
Tydide!
sentences.l:
O of the Danaans' race the bravest,
son of Tydeus!
sentences.i: O son of Tydeus, bravest of the Greeks!
sentences.n: Diomedes, son of Tydeus, fought Aeneas in Iliad 5 and would have killed him had Venus not carried her son from the field — the death Aeneas now wishes he had died. 'Tydide' is the vocative of 'Tydides', a Greek patronymic: 'son of Tydeus'. 'Danaum' = 'Danaorum'. 'fortissime' is vocative too, agreeing with 'Tydide'.

sentences.t:
Mene Iliacis occumbere campis
non potuisse, tuaque animam hanc effundere dextra,
saevus ubi Aeacidae telo iacet Hector, ubi ingens
Sarpedon, ubi tot Simois correpta sub undis
scuta virum galeasque et fortia corpora volvit?”
sentences.l:
That I on the Ilian plains to fall
should not have been able, and by your right hand pour out this life,
where fierce, by the weapon of Aeacus's grandson, lies Hector, where huge
Sarpedon lies, where so many, seized beneath its waves, the Simois
shields of men and helmets and brave bodies rolls?”
sentences.i: Why could I not have fallen on the plains of Ilium and poured out my life at your hand, where fierce Hector lies, brought down by the spear of Achilles, where huge Sarpedon lies, where the Simois sweeps beneath its waters and rolls along so many shields and helmets of men and the bodies of the brave?”
sentences.n: The accusative and infinitive of exclamation again — 'Mene… non potuisse', 'that I should not have been able…!' — the very construction of Juno's 'Mene… desistere' in line 37: hero and goddess open their speeches alike. 'Aeacidae' — 'the descendant of Aeacus' — is Achilles, his grandson, who killed Hector. Sarpedon, son of Jupiter, was killed by Patroclus. The Simois is a river of the Trojan plain. 'correpta' (seized, swept off) agrees with all three objects in the next line, 'scuta… galeas… corpora'. 'virum' = 'virorum'.
